text: A Money type that can't be added with plus, compared with equals, or printed with the stream operator forces every piece of code around it into awkward named function calls instead of natural expressions. Operator overloading lets your own types plug into C++'s built-in syntax — safely, and only where it actually makes code clearer.

Here, plus-equals is a member function that mutates the object directly, and plain plus is a free function built on top of it, taking its left operand by value so it has a safe copy to modify and return. Writing plus this way means the addition logic exists in exactly one place.

Equality should compare the actual data, not memory addresses, so operator equals is overloaded as a friend function that reaches into both objects' private members. C++20 adds the three-way comparison operator, nicknamed the spaceship operator, which can generate less-than, greater-than, and the rest from a single definition — and when you mark it default, the compiler compares every member in declaration order for you.

The stream insertion operator has to be a free function, full stop, because its left-hand operand is an ostream, not your type — you cannot add a member function to a class you don't own. Marking it a friend lets it still reach the private cents value to format the output.

Not every operator deserves overloading. Overload one only when its meaning is obvious — plus for addition, equals for equality — and reach for an ordinary named function anytime the behavior would surprise a reader. Clarity beats cleverness every time you're tempted to get creative with an operator's meaning.

Operator overloading lets a type like Money participate naturally in arithmetic, comparison, and stream syntax, as long as each overload stays intuitive and the stream operator stays a free function.
